Correct the student publicly with emphasis so that the repeated verb error becomes memorable for the whole class.
rationale: Feedback is most useful when selective, goal-aligned, understandable, and followed by an opportunity to notice and revise.
choiceRationales: Constant interruption disrupts fluency practice and overwhelms the learner, so feedback should be selective and purposeful.
A repeated error on the target verb deserves attention, and well-timed feedback can address form without discouraging participation.
Correct. Feedback is most useful when selective, goal-aligned, understandable, and followed by an opportunity to notice and revise.
Public shaming damages psychological safety and motivation, which undermines learning far more than it aids memory.

prompt: A lesson contains general academic verbs, technical nouns, and incidental decorative labels. Which planning move best supports academic vocabulary?
choices: Give equal instructional time to each unfamiliar word in the unit, including low-frequency details in the text.
Prioritize words central to the concept, teach them in networks and contexts, and plan repeated encounters.
Teach definitions of the unit words once in alphabetical order, then move on to the reading and discussion.
Delay content instruction until students have memorized the definition of each new word in the unit list.
rationale: Vocabulary selection considers conceptual importance, frequency, transfer, word families, and opportunities for meaningful repeated use.
choiceRationales: Spreading time equally across all words neglects the high-utility and conceptual terms that matter most for learning.
Correct. Vocabulary selection considers conceptual importance, frequency, transfer, word families, and opportunities for meaningful repeated use.
A single alphabetical presentation separates words from meaning and context and provides too few encounters for retention.
Memorization before content separates vocabulary from concepts, and academic words are learned best through repeated meaningful use.

prompt: A student has the same composite level as a peer yet different domain profiles and instructional needs. Which interpretation of proficiency levels is strongest?
choices: Assume the overall level defines each skill and predicts the learner’s future academic outcomes accurately.
Use the proficiency level as an indicator of the learner’s intelligence when planning course placements.
Treat bands as broad evidence within a multidimensional profile and examine skill and task performance.
Set aside classroom samples when they conflict with the score report, since standardized results are stronger.
rationale: Language proficiency varies by mode, purpose, context, genre, topic, and support; composite levels cannot replace detailed evidence.
choiceRationales: An overall level averages across domains, so it hides strengths and needs that the speaking and writing samples reveal.
Proficiency describes English development, not intelligence, and using it that way leads to inequitable and inaccurate placements.
Correct. Language proficiency varies by mode, purpose, context, genre, topic, and support; composite levels cannot replace detailed evidence.
Classroom samples add evidence about specific domains, so discarding them narrows an already broad overall score.

prompt: A learner waits to be called on rather than volunteering, and the teacher assumes lack of ideas. Which teacher response best supports cross-cultural interpretation?
choices: Suspend judgment, gather context, explain expectations, and offer multiple ways to show engagement.
Address the behavior right away with a consequence for disrespect, so classroom norms stay clear for all.
Assume that members of the student’s culture share this behavior and adjust expectations for the group.
Remove participation expectations for the student so the behavior no longer causes tension in class.
rationale: Observable behavior can carry different meanings across settings; educators investigate rather than pathologize and make hidden school norms transparent.
choiceRationales: Correct. Observable behavior can carry different meanings across settings; educators investigate rather than pathologize and make hidden school norms transparent.
Eye-contact norms vary across cultures, so punishing the behavior may misread a sign of respect as disengagement.
Generalizing to a whole culture stereotypes individuals, whose behavior may reflect many different personal and situational factors.
Dropping expectations lowers access to participation instead of explaining norms and offering respectful options for participation.

prompt: A colleague asks the ESOL teacher to determine special-education eligibility alone. Which response respects professional boundaries?
choices: Postpone any referral until the student’s English is fully developed, so language cannot explain the errors.
Confirm the disability diagnosis using the classroom English sample, since the error patterns are consistent.
Reassure the family that language learning explains the errors, ruling out the possibility of a disability.
Share specific observations, monitor language supports, and join the qualified team process without diagnosing.
rationale: Educators contribute evidence and support while disability evaluation and eligibility require authorized, nondiscriminatory multidisciplinary procedures.
choiceRationales: Evaluation should not be delayed until English is fully developed when there is reason to suspect a disability.
Diagnosis falls outside the teacher’s role and cannot rest on an English sample, which may reflect language difference.
Language learners can also have disabilities, so ruling it out without evaluation is equally outside the teacher’s role.
Correct. Educators contribute evidence and support while disability evaluation and eligibility require authorized, nondiscriminatory multidisciplinary procedures.

prompt: A direction says, "Teachers should discuss assignments with students in the library," and readers disagree about where the discussion occurs. Which analysis best explains the ambiguity?
choices: The sentence contains no possible syntactic ambiguity, so the disagreement reflects careless reading by some students.
The phrase can attach to more than one constituent, so reordering or repeating the noun removes the ambiguity.
The confusion comes from the formation of the letters on the printed notice rather than from the sentence structure.
Each reader should apply world knowledge in the same way, which would lead everyone to the same interpretation.
rationale: Attachment ambiguity arises when a phrase can modify different elements; revision should make the intended structural relationship explicit.
choiceRationales: Readers reach different meanings because the modifier can attach in two places, so the structure itself is genuinely ambiguous.
Correct. Attachment ambiguity arises when a phrase can modify different elements; revision should make the intended structural relationship explicit.
Letter formation does not change meaning here; the disagreement arises from how the phrase relates to the rest of the sentence.
World knowledge differs across readers and does not resolve structural ambiguity, which is why rewording the notice helps.

prompt: A learner sometimes produces third-person -s and sometimes omits it in similar contexts. Which interpretation of learner language is strongest?
choices: The alternation shows that the learner has no internal language system and is choosing past forms at random.
Variable forms show deliberate carelessness, so the learner should lose points each time an error appears.
Producing the correct irregular form once means that the learner has completed development of past tense.
Interlanguage is systematic yet variable, developing as learners test, revise, and automatize hypotheses.
rationale: Developing language reflects evolving internal patterns influenced by form, context, attention, input, and prior language knowledge.
choiceRationales: Overgeneralized forms like goed reveal a productive rule, which is evidence of an internal system rather than randomness.
Variability is a normal feature of developing language and does not indicate carelessness that warrants penalties.
Development continues after first correct use, and fluctuating forms show the system is still being restructured.
Correct. Developing language reflects evolving internal patterns influenced by form, context, attention, input, and prior language knowledge.

prompt: A project currently requires listening to a lecture and copying notes. Which plan best develops all four language domains?
choices: Add a separate activity for each language domain, even when the activities are unrelated to the unit’s ideas.
Treat listening, speaking, reading, and writing as isolated skills taught on different days without connections.
Sequence purposeful listening, speaking, reading, and writing around the same ideas toward independent production.
Assess the domain students find easiest, since high scores encourage learners to keep working in the unit.
rationale: Integrated modalities mirror academic communication and allow ideas and language to be encountered, negotiated, rehearsed, and expressed in connected ways.
choiceRationales: Unrelated activities fragment learning, whereas connected tasks let each domain reinforce the same content and language.
Domains support one another, so isolating them misses how input from reading and listening feeds speaking and writing.
Correct. Integrated modalities mirror academic communication and allow ideas and language to be encountered, negotiated, rehearsed, and expressed in connected ways.
Assessing the easiest domain hides needs in others and does not show whether the unit develops all four domains.

prompt: A district dashboard shows percentile rank beside performance descriptors tied to standards. Which choice best distinguishes norm- and criterion-referenced interpretations?
choices: Both results report raw counts of correct items, so they differ only in how the totals are formatted.
Criterion-referenced results rank students from highest to lowest relative to a representative group.
Norm-referenced results show mastery of each standard, while criterion results compare learners with peers.
Norm-referenced scores show relative standing; criterion-referenced scores show mastery against set targets.
rationale: The reference frame determines meaning: comparison with others differs from judgment against specified knowledge or performance criteria.
choiceRationales: The two results are interpreted differently, because one reports relative standing and the other reports whether defined expectations were met.
Ranking learners against a reference group describes norm-referenced interpretation, not comparison with defined criteria or expectations.
This reverses the definitions; norm-referenced results compare with peers and do not establish mastery of standards.
Correct. The reference frame determines meaning: comparison with others differs from judgment against specified knowledge or performance criteria.

prompt: Learners differ in comfort with interruption, silence, challenge, and public uncertainty. Which classroom discussion norm is strongest?
choices: Let the dominant interaction style continue without naming it, so discussions feel natural to most students.
Co-construct explicit norms for listening, entry, disagreement, evidence, and repair, and revisit participation.
Require each learner to contribute in the same way and amount starting with the next class discussion.
Avoid disagreement in discussions so that no student feels that their participation style is disrespected.
rationale: Inclusive norms make interactional expectations teachable, allow varied entry points, preserve intellectual challenge, and monitor equitable participation.
choiceRationales: Leaving the dominant style unnamed advantages some students and leaves others unsure how to enter or contribute to discussion.
Correct. Inclusive norms make interactional expectations teachable, allow varied entry points, preserve intellectual challenge, and monitor equitable participation.
Uniform requirements ignore different comfort levels and backgrounds, and abrupt demands can silence the learners they target.
Respectful disagreement is central to academic discussion, so avoiding it removes valuable opportunities to reason with evidence.

prompt: Staff place identifiable assessment results in a broadly accessible shared folder. Which privacy practice is strongest?
choices: Share only what legitimate professional responsibility requires, through secure, confidential channels.
Share student records with any school employee who asks, since all staff work toward student success.
Remove the student’s name from shared notes while keeping details that make the student easy to identify.
Post proficiency results publicly in the classroom to motivate students to improve their scores.
rationale: Professional collaboration requires purpose-limited, secure handling of personally identifiable information and respect for family and student privacy.
choiceRationales: Correct. Professional collaboration requires purpose-limited, secure handling of personally identifiable information and respect for family and student privacy.
Access to student records requires a legitimate educational interest, not simply employment somewhere in the school.
Removing a name while keeping obvious identifiers does not protect privacy, since the student remains identifiable.
Posting results publicly discloses protected information and can embarrass students publicly rather than motivate them to improve.

prompt: A student knows "act" but treats "action," "active," and "reactivate" as unrelated words. Which linguistic feature should be taught explicitly?
choices: Memorization of each printed word as a separate visual shape, without attention to shared parts across the words.
Final punctuation in sentences containing the words, since punctuation signals the grammatical role of each word.
Roots and derivational affixes, showing how morphology changes meaning and sometimes word class across a family.
Pronunciation practice for each word, assuming that saying the words correctly will supply their academic meanings.
rationale: Morphological awareness supports vocabulary growth by revealing recurring roots, prefixes, suffixes, meanings, and category changes.
choiceRationales: Treating related words as unrelated shapes hides the shared root that lets learners infer meaning across the word family.
Punctuation marks sentence boundaries and does not show how prefixes and suffixes alter word meaning or category.
Correct. Morphological awareness supports vocabulary growth by revealing recurring roots, prefixes, suffixes, meanings, and category changes.
Accurate pronunciation does not reveal how -ion, -able, and un- change meaning, which requires explicit morphological analysis.

prompt: Group members each hold one part of a diagram and must reconstruct the complete process. Which task best supports interaction?
choices: Use the information gap to require questions, clarification, and negotiated meaning with accountable roles.
Give each participant the completed schedule so the pair can agree on a time quickly without misunderstandings.
Allow participants to work on the task silently if they prefer, comparing written notes instead of talking.
Replace the schedule task with copying model dialogues so learners rehearse accurate sentences in their notebooks.
rationale: Information gaps create a communicative purpose and opportunities to negotiate meaning, receive feedback, and modify language.
choiceRationales: Correct. Information gaps create a communicative purpose and opportunities to negotiate meaning, receive feedback, and modify language.
Sharing the full schedule removes the information gap that makes questioning and negotiation of meaning necessary.
Silent note comparison avoids the spoken interaction the task is designed to promote, so learners lose speaking practice.
Copying dialogues provides form practice but creates no real exchange of information or negotiation of meaning between partners.

prompt: Students differ in literacy histories, home languages, and familiarity with the task. Which grouping plan is strongest?
choices: Keep beginning learners separated from proficient peers for the year so instruction can match their level.
Let the most fluent student in each group complete the shared tasks so the group produces accurate work.
Group students by home language for the year so they can always use their strongest language with peers.
Flexible, purpose-driven groups with explicit roles and language support, regrouped from evidence over time.
rationale: Grouping is instructional when tied to a purpose, balanced for participation and expertise, monitored, and changed as needs and tasks change.
choiceRationales: Permanent separation limits beginners’ access to proficient language models and to content-rich interaction with their peers.
Having one student do the work prevents others from practicing language and reasoning that group tasks should develop.
Same-language groups can help for some purposes, but fixed year-long grouping limits varied interaction and growth.
Correct. Grouping is instructional when tied to a purpose, balanced for participation and expertise, monitored, and changed as needs and tasks change.

prompt: The objective is to write a source-based historical argument for an academic audience. Which assessment is most authentic for the construct?
choices: Elicit the written source-based historical argument, scoring content and academic language criteria against the target.
Use an isolated word-matching quiz on the history vocabulary that appears in the source-based argument readings.
Measure silent reading speed on a textbook chapter as the main outcome for the historical argument writing task.
Ask students to rate how much they enjoyed the history unit and use the ratings as evidence of argument writing.
rationale: Performance assessment is appropriate when the construct involves integrated language use in a meaningful disciplinary task.
choiceRationales: Correct. Performance assessment is appropriate when the construct involves integrated language use in a meaningful disciplinary task.
Word matching checks isolated vocabulary recognition but does not show whether students can write a source-based historical argument for an academic audience.
The objective is writing a source-based historical argument, so silent reading speed measures an unrelated skill and misrepresents the construct.
Enjoyment ratings reflect attitudes and provide no evidence of the historical argument writing skills named in the objective.

prompt: A text treats one standardized English variety as evidence of intelligence and all others as broken language. Which response best addresses bias in materials?
choices: Keep the worksheet as published, since commercial materials undergo review and present neutral content.
Remove difficult topics from the unit without discussion so students are not exposed to biased framing.
Analyze whose knowledge is centered, revise deficit framing, and add counternarratives and critical awareness.
Ask multilingual students to explain why the worksheet is wrong about their families during class.
rationale: Materials communicate ideologies about language, identity, and power; critical selection and instruction can challenge inequitable representations.
choiceRationales: Published materials can contain bias, so assuming neutrality leaves the worksheet’s deficit framing unexamined and unchallenged.
Removing topics silently avoids the bias instead of teaching students to recognize, question, and challenge it.
Correct. Materials communicate ideologies about language, identity, and power; critical selection and instruction can challenge inequitable representations.
Asking marginalized students to defend their families places an unfair burden on them and can cause harm.

prompt: A social-media post says one instructional method works for every multilingual learner. Which use of research is most defensible?
choices: Adopt the program because the vendor’s confident claim suggests strong results in other districts.
Evaluate design, participants, measures, and limits; consider fit and equity; pilot and monitor outcomes.
Reject educational research entirely, since findings from other contexts rarely apply to local schools.
Use teacher testimonials from the vendor’s website as causal proof that the program improves fluency.
rationale: Evidence-informed practice combines critical appraisal with professional expertise, learner context, feasibility, equity, and local evaluation.
choiceRationales: Confidence is not evidence, and a guarantee of fluency in twelve weeks should prompt closer scrutiny, not adoption.
Correct. Evidence-informed practice combines critical appraisal with professional expertise, learner context, feasibility, equity, and local evaluation.
Context matters, but rejecting research altogether removes a key tool for judging programs and their likely effects.
Testimonials are selective and lack comparison groups, so they cannot establish that the program caused improvement.

prompt: A learner knows "could you" as separate words but misses it in natural conversation. Which response best addresses connected speech?
choices: Insisting that natural speech should match careful dictionary pronunciation so the learner hears each word clearly.
Teaching the names of isolated letters in going to, so the learner can spell the phrase while listening to speech.
Asking speakers to slow down in each future interaction with the learner so reduced forms are not heard at school.
Repeated listening with transcript support, marking reductions and linking, then fading the transcript over time.
rationale: Connected speech involves reduction, linking, stress, and rhythm; scaffolded perception practice builds access to authentic listening without freezing input at an artificial rate.
choiceRationales: Fluent speakers routinely reduce and link words, so expecting dictionary forms leaves the learner unprepared for real speech.
Letter names do not help the learner recognize the reduced spoken form, which is a listening and connected-speech skill.
Permanently slowing speech removes the input the learner needs to practice and does not build recognition of reduced forms.
Correct. Connected speech involves reduction, linking, stress, and rhythm; scaffolded perception practice builds access to authentic listening without freezing input at an artificial rate.

prompt: A student avoids speaking after repeated public correction despite understanding the lesson. Which motivation response is most defensible?
choices: Increase public correction of pronunciation until the student’s anxiety fades through repeated exposure.
Restore psychological safety with respectful norms, meaningful choice, attainable risk, and supportive feedback.
Treat the drop in participation as a fixed personality trait that classroom conditions are unlikely to change.
Remove the learner from peer interaction for the rest of the year to avoid further mocking by classmates.
rationale: Motivation and willingness to communicate are shaped by identity, safety, autonomy, perceived competence, relationships, and task value.
choiceRationales: Public correction after mockery intensifies embarrassment and anxiety, further discouraging the learner from speaking in front of peers.
Correct. Motivation and willingness to communicate are shaped by identity, safety, autonomy, perceived competence, relationships, and task value.
Motivation responds to classroom climate and relationships, so treating it as fixed ignores what teachers can change.
Isolation punishes the target of mockery and removes interaction that language learning depends on in the classroom.

prompt: A captioning and vocabulary tool could support a multimedia history lesson. Which plan appropriately uses technology?
choices: Evaluate alignment, accuracy, accessibility, privacy, and purpose, and teach students to verify tool output.
Adopt the newest translation tool available, since recent releases usually offer the best accuracy for students.
Upload identifiable student work to the tool without review so the program can personalize its language support.
Let the tool handle interaction and feedback during the task so the teacher can focus on grading afterward.
rationale: Technology is a means, not a goal; responsible use requires instructional fit, access, data safeguards, output verification, and attention to learner agency.
choiceRationales: Correct. Technology is a means, not a goal; responsible use requires instructional fit, access, data safeguards, output verification, and attention to learner agency.
Novelty does not ensure alignment with objectives or accuracy, so tools should be evaluated against the lesson purpose.
Uploading identifiable data without review risks violating the privacy laws and district procedures that protect students and families.
Tools cannot replace teacher interaction and feedback, which are central to language learning during collaborative tasks.

prompt: A team wants to use one language-proficiency score to decide disability eligibility without other evidence. Which concern should guide use of a standardized score?
choices: Treat the standardized reading score as a diagnosis that covers the learner’s collaboration skills as well.
Use the score for interpretations backed by its construct, norms, validity data, and authorized purpose.
Assume the numerical precision of the score removes uncertainty about the learner’s collaboration ability.
Use the reading score for any convenient classroom decision, since standardized scores are more objective.
rationale: Scores have bounded meanings; high-stakes interpretations require alignment, appropriate norms or criteria, multiple evidence, and qualified processes.
choiceRationales: A reading subtest does not measure collaboration, so treating it as a diagnosis extends the score beyond its construct.
Correct. Scores have bounded meanings; high-stakes interpretations require alignment, appropriate norms or criteria, multiple evidence, and qualified processes.
Precise-looking numbers still contain error and do not make an unsupported interpretation about classroom collaboration valid.
Standardized scores are valid only for supported purposes, and convenience does not justify uses outside that evidence.

prompt: A family wants help navigating school expectations but fears that success requires abandoning home practices. Which practice best supports acculturation without assimilation pressure?
choices: Encourage the newcomer to adopt an English-only identity outside school to speed adjustment to routines.
Expect adaptation to flow one way, with the newcomer changing while the school keeps its practices fixed.
Let the newcomer learn school norms through observation, avoiding explicit explanations that seem intrusive.
Teach routines explicitly, build reciprocal relationships, and preserve linguistic and cultural assets.
rationale: Adaptation is multidirectional and individual; additive support expands access while respecting identity, relationships, and community knowledge.
choiceRationales: Pressuring families toward English-only identities is assimilationist and weakens the newcomer’s valuable language and community ties.
Acculturation works best when schools also adapt and learn from families, rather than demanding one-way change.
Unexplained norms disadvantage newcomers, while explicit teaching gives them fair access to school expectations and choices.
Correct. Adaptation is multidirectional and individual; additive support expands access while respecting identity, relationships, and community knowledge.

prompt: A learner declines to translate sensitive family information for school staff. Which ethical response best supports student agency?
choices: Lower the student’s participation grade for declining to share the migration story with the class.
Ask the student to translate for newer classmates instead, since bilingual students can help in other ways.
Respect the boundary, provide alternative participation, avoid coercion, and avoid assigning adult roles.
Share the migration history anyway, since the example would help classmates understand the content.
rationale: Multilingual ability does not create an obligation to disclose identity or serve as interpreter; ethical practice protects consent, role, privacy, and equitable participation.
choiceRationales: Penalizing refusal coerces disclosure of personal history, which violates the student’s agency and right to privacy.
Assigning translation shifts an adult institutional role onto the student and does not respect the stated boundary.
Correct. Multilingual ability does not create an obligation to disclose identity or serve as interpreter; ethical practice protects consent, role, privacy, and equitable participation.
Sharing personal history against the student’s stated wishes breaches trust and can cause real emotional and social harm.

prompt: A learner confuses berry and very when listening and speaking. Which representation is most useful?
choices: An articulatory diagram or mirror comparing lip-teeth contact and airflow, practiced with meaningful minimal pairs.
Color coding the letters b and v with different colors that are unrelated to how either sound is produced in speech.
A description of b and v as having identical articulation, with the difference explained as a spelling convention.
Repetition of the target words at a louder volume, with the learner continuing until the sound seems correct.
rationale: Articulatory features plus perception and meaningful production can make an unfamiliar contrast observable and actionable.
choiceRationales: Correct. Articulatory features plus perception and meaningful production can make an unfamiliar contrast observable and actionable.
Colors can mark letters visually but provide no information about the bilabial stop versus labiodental fricative articulation that distinguishes /b/ and /v/.
The sounds /b/ (bilabial stop) and /v/ (labiodental fricative) differ in lip-teeth contact and continuous airflow, so describing them as identical misinforms the learner.
Volume does not change articulation, and repetition without feedback gives the learner no guidance about what to adjust.

prompt: Learners identify transition words on a worksheet but do not use them in oral explanations. Which learning sequence best supports automatization?
choices: Repeat one decontextualized drill item many times until the student can produce it without any hesitation.
Skip the explanation stage and demand fast responses from the start so students build speed under pressure.
Move from explicit noticing toward repeated meaningful retrieval in varied contexts with fading support.
Assess students on their written definitions of the grammar rule, since explaining it shows complete mastery.
rationale: Fluent access grows through meaningful, spaced, increasingly independent use after the form-function relationship is understood.
choiceRationales: Repeating one isolated item builds narrow recall that does not transfer to varied, meaningful role-play situations.
Demanding speed before understanding increases errors and anxiety, whereas automatization grows from repeated meaningful practice over time.
Correct. Fluent access grows through meaningful, spaced, increasingly independent use after the form-function relationship is understood.
Students can already explain the rule, so testing definitions ignores the real gap between knowledge and fluent use.

prompt: A multilingual student has a Section 504 plan affecting listening access. Which planning response best supports a learner with a documented disability?
choices: Suspend the IEP accommodations until the student’s English improves, since language may explain the difficulty.
Implement the current plan, coordinate language and specialized supports, and preserve the assessed construct.
Attribute the student’s difficulties to second-language learning and plan language supports in place of the IEP.
Allow the ESOL teacher to revise the accommodations independently when they seem unnecessary for a lesson.
rationale: Multilingual learners with disabilities need coordinated, individualized supports and valid access; educators implement authorized plans and contribute evidence within their roles.
choiceRationales: Accommodations in a current IEP must be implemented, and suspending them until English improves violates the plan.
Correct. Multilingual learners with disabilities need coordinated, individualized supports and valid access; educators implement authorized plans and contribute evidence within their roles.
The student has a documented disability, so treating all difficulty as language learning ignores legally required supports.
Changes to an IEP require the authorized team process, so one teacher cannot alter the legal plan or its accommodations alone.

prompt: A student receives extended processing time on a listening-response task under an approved plan. Which accommodation principle is most important?
choices: Each support offered to students is valid for each construct, so any accommodation can be used on any task.
Accommodations should raise scores whether or not they address an access need, since higher scores help.
The support should remove an access barrier without changing the essential construct and be documented.
Teachers may create new high-stakes accommodations after testing to adjust results that seem too low.
rationale: An accommodation supports access while preserving what is measured; appropriateness depends on construct, need, policy, and consistent implementation.
choiceRationales: Text-to-speech would alter a decoding construct, so whether a support is appropriate depends on what is measured.
Accommodations exist to provide access, not to inflate scores, so they must match a documented need.
Correct. An accommodation supports access while preserving what is measured; appropriateness depends on construct, need, policy, and consistent implementation.
High-stakes accommodations must follow authorized procedures before testing, not be invented afterward to change results that seem too low.

prompt: A teacher needs informed family participation in a consequential support meeting. Which family communication practice is most appropriate?
choices: Use qualified accessible interpretation or translation through approved procedures and verify understanding.
Ask the family’s young child to interpret the placement meeting, since the child speaks both languages well.
Send a machine translation of the placement notice without review, since it arrives quickly in the language.
Repeat the English explanation more slowly at the meeting, assuming this gives the caregivers meaningful access.
rationale: Consequential communication requires meaningful language access, accuracy, confidentiality, direct respect, and two-way participation.
choiceRationales: Correct. Consequential communication requires meaningful language access, accuracy, confidentiality, direct respect, and two-way participation.
Children should not interpret important school matters such as placement, which raises accuracy, confidentiality, and role concerns.
Unreviewed machine translation can introduce errors in high-stakes information, so qualified review is needed before sending it to families.
Slower English does not provide meaningful access for caregivers who have specifically requested communication in another language.

prompt: A district offers an English program but excludes learners from advanced courses and extracurricular activities. Which response best supports meaningful access?
choices: Allow students time to acquire English through exposure in grade-level classes before adding services.
Offer access to core classes and extracurriculars after students are reclassified as English proficient.
Provide identical materials without language support, treating equal materials as proof of equal access.
Provide an educationally sound, resourced language model with equitable access to core opportunities.
rationale: Equal opportunity requires effective language assistance and meaningful participation, not merely physical placement or formally identical treatment.
choiceRationales: Exposure to English without any services denies the language assistance learners need to participate in grade-level instruction meaningfully.
Waiting until reclassification withholds core opportunities that English learners are entitled to access while learning English.
Identical materials without support do not provide equal access when learners cannot yet understand the instruction delivered in English.
Correct. Equal opportunity requires effective language assistance and meaningful participation, not merely physical placement or formally identical treatment.

prompt: A learner answers "Do you have a pencil?" with yes but does not offer the pencil. Which concept is illustrated?
choices: The utterance has no communicative function beyond checking whether the learner hears the speaker clearly.
The literal form is a question, while its pragmatic function in this context is an indirect request.
The speaker is testing the learner’s knowledge of modal verb conjugation in a casual classroom exchange.
The response shows a phonemic contrast problem between can and could that changes the speaker’s meaning.
rationale: Pragmatic competence includes inferring speaker intent from form, relationship, setting, and shared conventions. The response connects linguistic or learner evidence with the language function, instructional or assessment purpose, multilingual assets, cultural context, professional role, access boundary, and an observable next step.
choiceRationales: The utterance clearly functions as a request for action, so saying it has no communicative function misses its purpose.

Correct. Pragmatic competence includes inferring speaker intent from form, relationship, setting, and shared conventions. The response connects linguistic or learner evidence with the language function, instructional or assessment purpose, multilingual assets, cultural context, professional role, access boundary, and an observable next step.
Nothing in the context suggests a grammar check; the speaker wants the window opened, which is a pragmatic function.
The learner understood the words correctly, so the issue is interpreting the intended function rather than hearing sounds.

prompt: An adult uses literacy and metalinguistic knowledge strategically but retains a noticeable accent. What is the strongest interpretation of age effects?
choices: Older learners lose the ability to acquire another language, so explicit grammar study is their sole option.
Younger learners progress faster in every language domain from the first day of exposure to the new language.
Accent is the best measure of overall proficiency, which explains why the younger sibling is more advanced.
Age interacts with experience, instruction, identity, exposure, and domain rather than fixing outcomes.
rationale: Age-related patterns differ across pronunciation, explicit learning, rate, ultimate attainment, context, and opportunity; deterministic claims are unwarranted.
choiceRationales: Adolescents and adults can acquire languages successfully, as the older learner’s rapid progress in explicit grammar study clearly shows.
Older learners often advance faster at first in some domains, so younger learners do not lead in every area initially.
Pronunciation is one domain of proficiency and does not capture grammar, vocabulary, literacy, or academic language.
Correct. Age-related patterns differ across pronunciation, explicit learning, rate, ultimate attainment, context, and opportunity; deterministic claims are unwarranted.

prompt: Learners practice explanations by reading identical completed answers to each other. Which plan makes student language use genuinely purposeful?
choices: Increase repetition of the unchanged scripted dialogue so students produce the request forms with more accuracy.
Remove the need to understand the partner by assigning each student a turn to read their lines aloud in order.
Create a real information or opinion gap with an audience, accountable roles, and support requiring negotiation.
Grade the role-play on speaking volume and clarity so that students project their voices during the activity.
rationale: Communicative tasks require a reason to exchange meaning, not merely oral production; accountability and scaffolds support equitable participation.
choiceRationales: Repeating a script with shared information builds rote accuracy but provides no genuine reason to communicate.
Reading lines in turn removes listening and negotiation, so the exchange stays mechanical rather than purposeful.
Correct. Communicative tasks require a reason to exchange meaning, not merely oral production; accountability and scaffolds support equitable participation.
Volume does not show communicative success, and grading it ignores whether students actually exchanged meaning with their partners.

prompt: Learners are developing oral explanations of cause and effect. Which formative assessment provides the best next-step evidence?
choices: A completion checklist recording which students turned in the comparison task by the end of the lesson.
A spelling quiz on unit vocabulary, used to estimate how well students justify comparisons with evidence.
An average of quiz scores from the unit, calculated without examining the reasoning in student responses.
A brief performance using the target function, analyzed with clear criteria to plan a reteach or extension.
rationale: Formative assessment must elicit the intended learning and yield interpretable evidence that changes instruction or learner strategy.
choiceRationales: Completion shows that work was submitted but reveals nothing about how well students justify comparisons with evidence.
Spelling accuracy is a different construct from using textual evidence to justify comparisons, so it misguides next steps.
Averages hide the specific strengths and needs in responses, which teachers must see to plan targeted reteaching.
Correct. Formative assessment must elicit the intended learning and yield interpretable evidence that changes instruction or learner strategy.

prompt: Caregivers rarely respond to one-way email messages sent only in English. Which engagement plan is most reciprocal?
choices: Send more reminders emphasizing that families who skip events are not supporting their children’s education.
Investigate access, schedules, and preferences, then offer varied channels and co-design meaningful roles.
Use attendance at the next evening event as the measure of how much each family cares about school.
Invite families to school when academic or behavior problems arise, so contacts focus on urgent needs.
rationale: Family engagement is relational and two-way; institutions examine their own barriers and value family expertise rather than equating visibility with commitment.
choiceRationales: Blame-based messages damage trust and ignore real, practical barriers such as work schedules, language, and transportation.
Correct. Family engagement is relational and two-way; institutions examine their own barriers and value family expertise rather than equating visibility with commitment.
Event attendance reflects access and timing, not caring, so it is a poor measure of family engagement.
Contact limited to problems makes engagement one-sided and negative, which discourages a lasting and trusting partnership with families.

prompt: Participation records show that English learners rarely access career programs with language-heavy application processes. Which advocacy approach is strongest?
choices: Document the barrier, center family views, analyze policy and data, propose changes, and monitor outcomes.
Publicly accuse individual teachers of bias without gathering evidence or proposing a workable remedy.
Speak on behalf of multilingual families in meetings without inviting them to share their own perspectives.
Lower the entry standards for advanced courses instead of removing the nomination barrier itself.
rationale: Effective advocacy is evidence-based, participatory, role-aware, solution-focused, and accountable for both access and outcomes.
choiceRationales: Correct. Effective advocacy is evidence-based, participatory, role-aware, solution-focused, and accountable for both access and outcomes.
Accusations made without evidence or workable solutions damage collaboration and leave the nomination-based screening barrier unchanged.
Speaking for families without inviting them excludes the people most affected and weakens the credibility of advocacy.
Lowering standards misidentifies the problem, which is an irrelevant screening barrier rather than the rigor of the program.

prompt: A student uses a casual greeting with a visiting official and is surprised by the reaction. What is the best instructional focus?
choices: Teach that formal register is morally superior and should replace casual speech with family and friends as well.
Focus on grammatical accuracy and set aside audience and purpose, since the answer was technically correct.
Compare register choices across relationships and settings without portraying any variety as deficient.
Require the learner to abandon home-language identities so that formal speech becomes natural in every setting.
rationale: Sociolinguistic competence involves choosing language suited to context while treating linguistic variation as systematic and identity-linked.
choiceRationales: Registers are suited to different contexts, and framing one as morally superior devalues the learner’s home communities.
The answer was already correct; the issue is how audience and purpose shape tone, which is precisely what register addresses.
Correct. Sociolinguistic competence involves choosing language suited to context while treating linguistic variation as systematic and identity-linked.
Adding registers does not require giving up identity, and demanding that loss harms motivation and belonging.

prompt: Learners copy a new term but never encounter its word family, collocations, or disciplinary uses. Which practice best supports durable vocabulary growth?
choices: Repeated encounters across modes and contexts linking form and meaning, word parts, set phrases, and use.
A single exposure in a definition list, followed by a test months later to measure long-term retention.
An approximate translation of each word given without context, so students can move quickly through the list.
Moving on from words once they are introduced, so class time focuses on new vocabulary rather than review.
rationale: Vocabulary depth and retention develop through multiple meaningful encounters, retrieval, semantic connections, morphology, and productive use.
choiceRationales: Correct. Vocabulary depth and retention develop through multiple meaningful encounters, retrieval, semantic connections, morphology, and productive use.
One encounter is rarely enough for durable learning; words need multiple meaningful exposures and retrieval practice.
Translations can help initially, but without context learners miss collocations, register, and nuances of academic use.
Without revisiting words, learners tend to forget them, while spaced encounters and use strengthen long-term vocabulary knowledge.

prompt: Learners use evidence stems only during one teacher-led discussion. Which unit plan best supports transfer?
choices: Keep the worksheet prompt and context identical across the unit so students become confident using the phrases.
Treat one correct worksheet response as evidence that students will use the transition phrases in later writing.
Remove feedback early in the unit so students learn to choose transition phrases without relying on the teacher.
Model the language in varied disciplinary tasks, guide retrieval, fade scaffolds, and assess independent use.
rationale: Transfer grows when learners recognize deep functions, retrieve language in varied contexts, receive feedback, and gain independent control.
choiceRationales: Identical prompts build narrow performance, so students may not recognize when to use the phrases in new contexts.
A single correct response in one format does not show independent use, which requires varied practice and assessment.
Feedback is needed until learners understand each function, and withdrawing it early can entrench misuse of phrases.
Correct. Transfer grows when learners recognize deep functions, retrieve language in varied contexts, receive feedback, and gain independent control.

prompt: A digital portfolio includes many files but no dates, criteria, or reflection. Which portfolio practice is strongest?
choices: Purposeful samples across time and modes with shared rubrics, self-review, feedback, and a clear purpose.
A large collection of files, with the number of pieces treated as an indicator of the learner’s proficiency.
A set of polished final products, with drafts and revisions removed so the folder shows the learner’s best.
A folder used for each placement and exit decision without validating it for those high-stakes purposes.
rationale: Portfolios can show development and performance breadth when evidence is systematically selected, contextualized, evaluated, and interpreted.
choiceRationales: Correct. Portfolios can show development and performance breadth when evidence is systematically selected, contextualized, evaluated, and interpreted.
Quantity of work does not show proficiency or growth, so file counts give little interpretable evidence.
Removing drafts hides growth and revision, which are among the most valuable kinds of portfolio evidence.
Portfolios need validation before supporting high-stakes decisions, so using them for every purpose without evidence is unjustified.

prompt: Families and community partners hold knowledge relevant to a unit on systems, migration, or environmental change. Which use of community knowledge best supports instruction?
choices: Use community stories as decoration for bulletin boards without connecting them to the unit’s objectives.
Require students to share private family information so lessons reflect each household’s experiences.
Connect funds of knowledge to rigorous objectives with consent and reciprocity, without exhibiting learners.
Keep school knowledge and community knowledge separate, since academic standards define the curriculum.
rationale: Funds-of-knowledge approaches build on historically accumulated household and community expertise while preserving dignity, choice, and academic purpose.
choiceRationales: Decorative use treats community knowledge as display rather than as a resource connected to rigorous learning objectives.
Requiring private information violates family privacy and consent, which funds-of-knowledge work must respect at every stage.
Correct. Funds-of-knowledge approaches build on historically accumulated household and community expertise while preserving dignity, choice, and academic purpose.
Community expertise can deepen academic learning, so keeping the two separate wastes valuable resources that learners bring.

prompt: A school judges effectiveness from one year of English-language arts grades without comparison or implementation data. Which program-evaluation design is most useful?
choices: Count the students exited from services each year as the single measure of the program’s success.
Examine proficiency growth, content outcomes, fidelity, subgroups, and family input over time.
Choose the easiest positive indicator, such as celebration attendance, to report program effectiveness.
Skip checking whether services were implemented and focus on end-of-year test scores in the report.
rationale: Program evaluation requires multiple aligned outcomes and process evidence, disaggregation, stakeholder perspectives, longitudinal patterns, and response to findings.
choiceRationales: Exit counts alone can hide weak content outcomes or premature exits, so multiple indicators are needed.
Correct. Program evaluation requires multiple aligned outcomes and process evidence, disaggregation, stakeholder perspectives, longitudinal patterns, and response to findings.
Easy positive indicators show little about learning or access and can mask real weaknesses in the ESOL program.
Without implementation data, the district cannot tell whether results reflect the program itself or its absence.

prompt: A peer says, "You might want to check that," intending advice, but the learner treats it as optional small talk. Which analysis best explains the misunderstanding?
choices: The words in the comment carry no meaning by themselves, so the learner could not have interpreted the remark.
The learner must have difficulty decoding print, which would explain why the spoken comment was misunderstood.
Pronunciation features alone explain how implied stance is communicated, so intonation drills will resolve it.
The learner needs support interpreting indirect stance, mitigation, and contextual cues, not vocabulary alone.
rationale: Meaning extends beyond dictionary definitions to implicature, politeness, prosody, relationship, and discourse context. The response connects linguistic or learner evidence with the language function, instructional or assessment purpose, multilingual assets, cultural context, professional role, access boundary, and an observable next step.
choiceRationales: The words do carry meaning; the learner took their literal positive sense and missed the implied criticism in context.
The comment was spoken, so decoding print is unrelated; the gap is interpreting indirect, mitigated feedback.
Intonation can signal stance, but understanding implied criticism also depends on context, the speakers’ relationship, and cultural conventions.

Correct. Meaning extends beyond dictionary definitions to implicature, politeness, prosody, relationship, and discourse context. The response connects linguistic or learner evidence with the language function, instructional or assessment purpose, multilingual assets, cultural context, professional role, access boundary, and an observable next step.

prompt: A French-speaking learner recognizes many academic cognates yet occasionally transfers a misleading look-alike. Which interpretation best uses cross-linguistic knowledge?
choices: Ban use of the first language during reading so the learner stops relying on cross-language connections.
Teach strategic cognate use while explicitly checking meaning, form, and false cognates in context.
Assume that similar-looking words share the same meaning across both languages, including false cognates.
Treat cross-language connections as a shortcut that avoids real learning and discourage them in class.
rationale: Prior-language knowledge can accelerate learning when used strategically and verified; transfer may be positive or misleading.
choiceRationales: Cognates are a powerful resource for Spanish speakers, so banning the first language discards a proven reading strategy.
Correct. Prior-language knowledge can accelerate learning when used strategically and verified; transfer may be positive or misleading.
False cognates show that similarity does not ensure shared meaning, so learners need to verify meaning in context.
Cross-linguistic connections support vocabulary and comprehension and should be taught strategically rather than discouraged as a shortcut.

prompt: Learners identify historical events but cannot explain relationships among causes and consequences. Which teacher move best scaffolds a complex explanation?
choices: Model the discourse, jointly construct an example, offer a temporary frame, and fade support with performance.
Supply a completed model paragraph for students to keep using whenever they write explanations in the unit.
Lower the task to copying definitions of the labels so students can show their knowledge of the science model.
Focus feedback on handwriting and neatness so students present their labeled diagrams more clearly to readers.
rationale: Effective scaffolding is contingent, explicit, and temporary; it supports the intended reasoning and language before responsibility shifts to learners.
choiceRationales: Correct. Effective scaffolding is contingent, explicit, and temporary; it supports the intended reasoning and language before responsibility shifts to learners.
A permanent model encourages copying rather than building the students’ ability to construct causal explanations independently.
Copying definitions removes the causal reasoning students already understand and does not scaffold the connected explanation they need to write.
Handwriting feedback does not address the gap between labels and connected causal explanation in the writing.

prompt: A writing rubric combines content, organization, vocabulary, grammar, and mechanics into one vague impression. Which rubric design best supports useful feedback?
choices: Criteria based on personality traits such as confidence and friendliness that the teacher observes in class.
Observable, task-aligned criteria with clear performance descriptions and exemplars, applied consistently.
Criteria kept private until after scoring so that students focus on speaking naturally during the task.
Standards adjusted informally for each student’s situation without documentation of the changes made.
rationale: Transparent analytic criteria improve alignment, feedback specificity, learner self-assessment, and scoring consistency.
choiceRationales: Personality traits are not speaking skills, so they produce biased scores and feedback unrelated to language goals.
Correct. Transparent analytic criteria improve alignment, feedback specificity, learner self-assessment, and scoring consistency.
Hidden criteria prevent students from knowing what quality looks like, which undermines useful feedback and growth.
Undocumented changes make scores inconsistent and unfair, so results cannot be interpreted or compared across students.

prompt: A teacher interprets indirect caregiver questions as agreement, but the family remains concerned. Which response best handles a cultural misunderstanding?
choices: Explain that the teacher’s intent was efficiency, so the family should reinterpret the feedback accordingly.
Attribute the conflict to the family’s cultural expectations, which differ from the school’s practices.
Limit future communication with the family to written notices so misunderstandings are less likely.
Clarify intent and interpretation respectfully, invite their view, repair impact, and set a clearer process.
rationale: Cross-cultural repair requires curiosity, attention to impact and power, explicit meaning, and a reciprocal communication plan.
choiceRationales: Focusing only on intent dismisses the impact on the family and prevents mutual understanding and repair.
Blaming one culture for the conflict is a deficit view and ignores the shared responsibility for communication.
Reducing communication to written notices weakens the partnership and leaves the original misunderstanding unresolved for both sides.
Correct. Cross-cultural repair requires curiosity, attention to impact and power, explicit meaning, and a reciprocal communication plan.

prompt: A newcomer schedule isolates students from grade-level content and extracurricular activities without individualized educational justification. Which response best addresses unnecessary segregation?
choices: Assume that a separate classroom is the safer setting for English learners and maintain the current schedule.
End targeted language instruction for the students regardless of need so they can join general classes.
Review whether separation is justified, limited, effective, and reevaluated while expanding integration.
Justify the separate placement by scheduling convenience, since moving students would complicate timetables.
rationale: Language services may require targeted support, but exclusion should not exceed what is educationally justified and must not deny meaningful opportunities.
choiceRationales: Separation must be educationally justified and limited, so assuming it is safer ignores access to peers and electives.
Learners who still need language instruction should receive it, so ending all services overcorrects the segregation problem.
Correct. Language services may require targeted support, but exclusion should not exceed what is educationally justified and must not deny meaningful opportunities.
Convenience is not an educational justification and does not satisfy legal obligations to avoid unnecessary segregation.

prompt: An oral explanation contains accurate facts but shifts topics without reference words or transitions. Which feature creates cohesion?
choices: Teach how referents, lexical ties, substitution, and connectors link ideas across sentences into connected text.
Add more relevant facts to each paragraph so the essay feels complete even if the sentences remain unconnected.
Focus feedback on handwriting legibility, since neater writing helps readers follow the relationships between ideas.
Require each sentence in the paragraph to begin with the same transition word so the ideas appear clearly linked.
rationale: Cohesion uses linguistic ties across clauses and sentences, while coherence depends on an interpretable overall organization and relationship among ideas.
choiceRationales: Correct. Cohesion uses linguistic ties across clauses and sentences, while coherence depends on an interpretable overall organization and relationship among ideas.
More facts increase length but do not create the ties between sentences that make an essay read as connected discourse.
Legibility affects how easily a reader decodes the essay but does not supply reference, repetition, or connectors that create cohesion.
Repeating one transition mechanically ignores logical relationships and does not teach the full range of cohesive devices.

prompt: Partners compare a concept in home-language notes and then co-construct an English summary. Which response treats multilingualism as an asset?
choices: Require learners to set aside all known languages before planning so English becomes the language of thought.
Record home-language use during planning as off-task behavior that lowers the participation grade for the day.
Permit purposeful use of the full linguistic repertoire to develop ideas while keeping the English outcome.
Replace the English presentation objective with a translation task completed in the students’ home languages.
rationale: Strategic multilingual practices can support cognition, identity, collaboration, and transfer while instruction still targets clear English outcomes.
choiceRationales: Suppressing known languages limits complex thinking, while translanguaging during planning can deepen and organize students’ ideas.
Using home languages to plan is purposeful learning, so penalizing it treats a multilingual asset as misconduct.
Correct. Strategic multilingual practices can support cognition, identity, collaboration, and transfer while instruction still targets clear English outcomes.
Translation alone abandons the English-language outcome, whereas the asset-based approach keeps the English presentation goal in place.

prompt: A lesson relies on teacher talk followed by chorus repetition from the whole class. Which interaction pattern gives the strongest evidence of learning?
choices: Call on the fastest speakers in the class so the lesson keeps moving and other students hear correct answers.
Extended wait time, varied participation structures, probing questions, peer uptake, and prompts to explain.
Treat strong choral responses as proof that each student understands the content being reviewed in the lesson.
Answer each question yourself after a short pause so students hear an accurate model of the expected response.
rationale: Interaction supports development when learners have equitable time and responsibility to formulate, extend, negotiate, and respond to ideas.
choiceRationales: Relying on quick volunteers excludes learners who need processing time, so the teacher gathers evidence from only a few.
Correct. Interaction supports development when learners have equitable time and responsibility to formulate, extend, negotiate, and respond to ideas.
Choral volume hides individual misunderstanding, so it cannot show what each learner in the class actually knows.
Answering for students removes their chance to produce language and gives the teacher no evidence of learning.

prompt: Students misuse past tense in spontaneous discussion but succeed during edited writing. Which analysis best uses error data?
choices: Count each article omission as the same error and give all learners the identical review lesson on articles.
Infer each learner’s motivation from a single response and assign extra practice to those who seem careless.
Classify patterns by form, function, context, frequency, communicative effect, and development before teaching.
Teach a rule about verb tense, since the omissions suggest a general weakness in English grammar overall.
rationale: Error analysis becomes instructionally useful when it identifies systematic conditions and the language function rather than merely tallying differences.
choiceRationales: The omissions differ by noun type, task, and attention, so treating them as one error misses distinct instructional needs.
One response cannot reveal motivation, and the varied patterns point to developmental and contextual factors instead.
Correct. Error analysis becomes instructionally useful when it identifies systematic conditions and the language function rather than merely tallying differences.
Teaching an unrelated rule ignores the article patterns in the data and does not address the actual learner needs.

prompt: A volunteer program asks for unrestricted student records to coordinate services. Which partnership safeguard is most important?
choices: Define purpose, use authorized consent, minimize and secure data, vet partners, and evaluate benefit and risk.
Share all requested student information because the tutoring program is free and intended to help learners.
Allow the community partner to set its own privacy rules for handling student data during the program.
Accept the organization’s verbal promise of confidentiality instead of following approved data procedures.
rationale: Community partnership does not remove privacy, consent, safety, role, accessibility, data minimization, oversight, or evaluation obligations.
choiceRationales: Correct. Community partnership does not remove privacy, consent, safety, role, accessibility, data minimization, oversight, or evaluation obligations.
A free service does not override privacy obligations, and immigration details carry serious risks for families.
Schools remain responsible for student privacy, so partners cannot set their own rules for protected data.
Verbal promises provide no enforceable protection, so approved data agreements and procedures are required before sharing.

prompt: A family declines a designated class but the learner continues to need access to instruction. Which response best serves a family that declines a particular EL service?
choices: Remove language support entirely after the opt-out, since the family declined the offered program.
Insist that the family accept the offered program model, since it is the district’s standard service.
Treat the opt-out as permanent evidence that the student no longer needs language support or monitoring.
Explain options accessibly, honor rights, keep meeting federal language duties, and monitor progress.
rationale: Declining a particular service does not erase the school's responsibility to provide meaningful access, communicate rights, and monitor whether the learner is progressing.
choiceRationales: Declining a program does not end the school’s obligation to provide language access and monitor progress.
Families have the right to decline particular services, so forcing acceptance of one model disregards that right.
Opting out reflects a family choice, not a change in need, so monitoring and support obligations continue.
Correct. Declining a particular service does not erase the school's responsibility to provide meaningful access, communicate rights, and monitor whether the learner is progressing.

prompt: A learner encounters "pitch" in music, sports, and marketing texts. Which distinction is most useful?
choices: Assume that each English word has one core meaning and teach that meaning before introducing other senses later.
Use context and semantic fields to select among a word’s multiple meanings while noting its conventional uses.
Choose the longest dictionary entry for the word regardless of context, since it includes the most common sense.
Treat the multiple meanings of the word as spelling errors that the learner should correct during proofreading.
rationale: Lexical meaning is context-sensitive; instruction should help learners use surrounding syntax, topic, collocation, and semantic relationships.
choiceRationales: Many common words have multiple meanings, and the learner already knows two; the need is choosing the right one in context.
Correct. Lexical meaning is context-sensitive; instruction should help learners use surrounding syntax, topic, collocation, and semantic relationships.
Entry length does not indicate which sense fits a sentence, so context rather than length must guide meaning selection.
Multiple meanings are a normal feature of the lexicon, not errors, and the spelling of the word is the same in both senses.

prompt: A learner omits subjects in English because the first language permits information to be recovered from verb forms. Which analysis best explains transfer?
choices: Conclude that the learner does not understand syntax and needs to restart basic sentence-structure lessons.
Correct the adjective position each time it appears without giving examples or explaining the English pattern.
Attribute each error in the learner’s writing to first-language transfer and plan instruction around that view.
Compare the language systems and use the pattern for targeted contrastive noticing, not as a global deficit.
rationale: Cross-linguistic influence can explain some systematic patterns, but teachers verify rather than presume the source and teach the specific contrast.
choiceRationales: The learner is applying a real syntactic pattern from another language, which shows syntactic knowledge, not its absence.
Correction without explanation gives little insight into why the pattern differs, so noticing and examples are needed.
Transfer explains some errors, but others arise from developmental patterns, so attributing every error to it is inaccurate.
Correct. Cross-linguistic influence can explain some systematic patterns, but teachers verify rather than presume the source and teach the specific contrast.

prompt: Following a demonstration, students say yes when asked whether the process is clear. Which response best checks comprehension?
choices: Repeat the question about understanding more loudly so that each student responds clearly and confidently.
Treat the silence and nodding as confirmation that the class understands the direction and can start work.
Ask learners to restate, sequence, demonstrate, or begin the task while observing evidence and reteaching.
Wait until the unit test to find out whether students understood the directions given during the lesson.
rationale: Comprehension checks require observable evidence aligned to the meaning or action, not self-report under social pressure.
choiceRationales: Yes–no questions invite nodding regardless of understanding, so asking the same question louder produces no better evidence.
Learners may nod to be polite or avoid embarrassment, so nodding is not reliable evidence of comprehension.
Correct. Comprehension checks require observable evidence aligned to the meaning or action, not self-report under social pressure.
Waiting for the test delays correction until misunderstanding has already affected students’ work throughout the unit.

prompt: A reading task assumes niche cultural knowledge unrelated to the stated standard. Which response best protects assessment fairness?
choices: Remove authentic accent variation from listening tasks so recordings use one standardized broadcast voice.
Assume that identical administration for each student ensures that scores are fair and valid for all groups.
Lower comprehension expectations for students from one identity group to compensate for the unfamiliar accent.
Review representation, language load, accessibility, and construct relevance, revising barriers not essential.
rationale: Fairness requires access to the intended construct and scrutiny of irrelevant barriers, while authentic variation may remain when it is part of the construct.
choiceRationales: Some variation is authentic and valuable, so the goal is to align accents with the construct rather than remove variety.
Identical administration does not remove construct-irrelevant barriers, so equal conditions alone do not ensure validity for all students.
Lowering expectations for a group is inequitable and leaves the construct-irrelevant barrier in the quiz unaddressed.
Correct. Fairness requires access to the intended construct and scrutiny of irrelevant barriers, while authentic variation may remain when it is part of the construct.

prompt: A learner writes "do a decision" and "powerful tea" even though each individual word is familiar. Which teaching move best develops collocational knowledge?
choices: Mark each unusual phrase as wrong in the essay without showing the learner which combinations are typically used.
Teach new vocabulary words in alphabetical lists so the learner masters individual meanings before combining them.
Use authentic or corpus examples to notice common word partnerships, compare options, and practice them in chunks.
Explain that word combinations follow fixed grammar rules that apply the same way across contexts and genres.
rationale: Collocations are conventional patterns not fully predictable from individual meanings; noticing and retrieval of chunks support fluent, appropriate use.
choiceRationales: Marking errors without models leaves the learner guessing, since collocations are learned by noticing typical partnerships.
Alphabetical isolation separates words from the partners they appear with, which is the knowledge the learner lacks.
Correct. Collocations are conventional patterns not fully predictable from individual meanings; noticing and retrieval of chunks support fluent, appropriate use.
Collocations are conventional and vary by genre and context, so presenting them as fixed grammar rules is misleading.

prompt: A multilingual learner uses different words and routines across home, school, and community settings. Which conclusion about bilingual development is most accurate?
choices: Evaluate knowledge spanning languages and contexts, since distributed competence may not show in one language.
Add the vocabulary counts from both languages without checking for duplicate concepts and report it as official.
Interpret the distributed knowledge as confusion between languages that slows the child’s overall development.
Assess vocabulary in the child’s less familiar context alone, since that shows the child’s weakest area clearly.
rationale: Bilingual knowledge can be distributed by person, setting, topic, and language; interpretation should match the construct and purpose of assessment.
choiceRationales: Correct. Bilingual knowledge can be distributed by person, setting, topic, and language; interpretation should match the construct and purpose of assessment.
Simple addition can double-count concepts, and an informal sum should not be presented as an official standardized score.
Knowing some concepts in one language and some in both is typical bilingual development, not a sign of confusion.
Assessing only the less familiar context underestimates what the child knows and misses the competence distributed across both languages.

prompt: A student gives a strong oral explanation but repeatedly omits the language form targeted in the lesson. Which feedback most supports revision?
choices: Mark every language difference in the paragraph with equal weight so the learner sees all errors at once.
Rewrite the learner’s paragraph in the teacher’s own words to model how the ideas should be expressed.
Praise the learner’s effort warmly while leaving out specific information about the language patterns.
Acknowledge the meaning, target one or two patterns, prompt self-correction, and allow refinement.
rationale: Actionable feedback is selective, specific, connected to objectives, and followed by learner processing and another performance opportunity.
choiceRationales: Marking everything equally overwhelms the learner and hides the two patterns that matter most for this revision.
Replacing the learner’s writing removes ownership and the chance to practice revising reference and sentence boundaries.
Praise without information gives no guidance on what to change, so the recurring patterns are likely to persist.
Correct. Actionable feedback is selective, specific, connected to objectives, and followed by learner processing and another performance opportunity.

prompt: Teachers compare domain scores with observations, portfolios, and opportunity-to-learn information. Which data conversation is most defensible?
choices: Triangulate converging and conflicting evidence, note limits, engage families, and stay within the record.
Let the language-proficiency score override the other sources, since it is the most standardized measure.
Select evidence that supports the team’s initial view so the meeting reaches a decision efficiently.
Share identifiable results with interested staff members so more adults can support the learners.
rationale: Multiple measures can strengthen decisions when their constructs and limitations are understood and privacy, role, and stakeholder participation are respected.
choiceRationales: Correct. Multiple measures can strengthen decisions when their constructs and limitations are understood and privacy, role, and stakeholder participation are respected.
One score cannot capture the full picture, so letting it override other evidence narrows the basis for decisions.
Choosing only confirming evidence produces confirmation bias and can lead the team to inaccurate or inequitable decisions.
Results should be shared only with those who have a legitimate educational need, under privacy laws and procedures.

prompt: In group work, a student waits indefinitely because entry phrases and floor-taking signals are unclear. Which discourse feature needs support?
choices: Assign silent grammar worksheets during discussion time so the learner practices accuracy before speaking again.
Label the behavior as disrespectful in a behavior report without investigating the conventions the learner knows.
Eliminate collaborative talk from lessons so the learner is not placed in situations requiring turn-taking cues.
Model and rehearse topic shifts, joining stems, turn cues, and repair across authentic interaction settings.
rationale: Interactional competence includes managing turns, topics, repair, and participation; conventions vary and should be made visible rather than moralized.
choiceRationales: Worksheets do not teach how to enter, shift, or yield turns, which are interactional skills learned through practice.
